# What a year of fixing bicycles taught me about my old job

I quit my product manager job on a Tuesday in March, gave two weeks' notice, and by the following month I was standing behind the counter at Wheelhouse Cycles asking my new boss, Dave, how to true a wheel. I did not have a plan beyond that. I had a savings cushion, a growing suspicion that I'd forgotten what it felt like to finish something, and an ad on the shop's Instagram looking for part-time help that I'd been staring at for three weeks before I finally called.

People ask why I left, expecting a story about a bad manager or a burnout diagnosis, and honestly there wasn't one dramatic moment. It was more like a slow leak. I'd spent six years managing a suite of internal tools nobody outside the company had heard of, and somewhere in year four I noticed that I could describe exactly what I'd shipped in a quarter and still not point to anything I could touch. Roadmaps got reprioritized. Features I'd fought for got cut two sprints before launch because a VP changed their mind in a meeting I wasn't in. I'd sit in retros where we'd talk about "impact" using numbers that were themselves modeled estimates of other estimates. At some point I realized I hadn't made anything with my hands since I helped my brother put together an IKEA dresser two Christmases earlier, and that thought bothered me more than it should have.

So I left, and I fixed bikes for a year.

## What the days actually looked like

The shop was small — three of us on a normal day, four during the spring rush — wedged between a laundromat and a taqueria on a street that floods a little every time it rains hard. Dave had owned it for eleven years and could true a wheel blindfolded, which I know because I watched him do most of one while telling a story about a customer's dog. My first few weeks I did almost nothing but patch tubes and adjust brakes, over and over, until my hands stopped feeling clumsy around a tire lever. Then came the flat-repair rush of the mornings, the tune-up backlog that built up every Thursday for reasons nobody ever explained, and the occasional frame that came in so neglected the chain had essentially fused itself to the cassette.

Here is what nobody tells you about bike repair: most of it is diagnosis, not wrenching. A customer comes in and says their bike makes a clicking sound, and the actual repair might take four minutes once you find it, but finding it can take twenty. You ride it around the block. You isolate variables — pedal while coasting, stand up, sit down, shift through the gears one at a time listening for where the sound changes. It's closer to debugging than I expected, except the feedback loop is a sound in your ear instead of a log file, and when you fix it, you fix it. There's no PR review. There's no "let's revisit this next sprint." The customer rides off five minutes later and the click is gone or it isn't, and you know immediately which.

I also learned that the job is maybe forty percent bicycles and sixty percent talking to people about their bicycles, which took some adjusting to. Regulars would come by just to hang around while we worked. A woman named Priya brought us banana bread twice a month like clockwork and would sit on the stool by the register recapping her group ride mishaps while I trued her wheel. It was a different kind of social contract than open-plan office small talk — nobody was building a personal brand or angling for a promotion. People were just there because their bike was broken and they wanted it not to be.

## Two repairs I still think about

There was a man, Harold, who brought in a Raleigh three-speed that had belonged to his father. The frame was a mess of surface rust, the shifter cable had basically disintegrated, and the leather saddle had gone stiff as a board. He wasn't looking for a full restoration and he wasn't precious about originality — he just wanted to be able to ride it to the pharmacy a mile from his house without something falling apart underneath him. We spent two afternoons on it, mostly me, with Dave checking in periodically to make sure I wasn't overtightening anything on a sixty-year-old frame. When Harold came to pick it up, he rode it in a slow circle in the parking lot, got off, and just said, "Well, look at that," in a voice that made the whole two days worth it. I didn't get a Slack message with a thumbs-up emoji. I got a guy in his seventies grinning at a bike his dad used to ride.

The other one that sticks with me is less sentimental and more instructive. A courier named Marcus came in on a Friday afternoon, bike making a horrible grinding noise, and he needed it fixed in the next forty minutes because he was still on shift and losing money every minute he wasn't riding. His bottom bracket was shot. There was no elegant version of this repair — I had to just do it, fast, with him standing there watching the clock. It taught me something about the difference between working under artificial urgency, which had defined most of my old job's fire drills, and working under real urgency, where the stakes were obvious to everyone in the room and nobody needed a status update to understand why it mattered.

## Going back to an office

I'm back in product management now, at a different company, and I won't pretend the year in the shop transformed me into some Zen wrench-wielding sage. I still sit in meetings that go long. I still write documents that get read by four people and referenced by zero. But I notice things I didn't notice before. I notice when a project has gone so long without anyone actually seeing the thing work that we've forgotten what "done" is supposed to feel like. I push harder now for demos over decks, for smaller loops between building something and watching a real person react to it. I also just have more patience for the parts of the job that are genuinely tedious, because tedious was ninety percent of what fixing bikes actually was, and I'd rather be tediously useful than abstractly aspirational.

Mostly, though, I think about Harold's grin more than I think about any dashboard I ever shipped. That's probably the whole point.
